INTERPRETATION OF STANDING ORDER 41 RESPECTING THE TABUING OF DOCUMENTS CITED AND LETTERS QUOTED
speechtext:
On Wednesday last,
March 5, I was asked by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) to take into consideration standing order 41 and give an interpretation particularly of paragraphs 315 and 316 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, which deal with the question of the reading of documents and whether these documents should: be laid on the table. When the hon. member made the suggestion I indicated that it was not the function of the chair to give advice to hon. members but rather that the Speaker was required to judge and interpret the rules of the house on any question raised in the course of a debate or in its proceedings.
The hon. member had in mind the discussion which took place that day and which had just been completed, on the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen), in the course of which she read a letter received from a correspondent. It might be well to state to
the house the rule governing questions of privilege. It has been well stated in May's Parliamentary Practice, 13th edition, page 317: The house is always willing to extend its indulgence when an honourable member wishes to clear up any misrepresentation of his character: but that indulgence ought to be strictly limited to such misrepresentations, and ought not to extend to any observations other than by way of correction.
It was not necessary for me to give a decision during the discussion for the reason that the hon. member for North Battleford agreed >to lay on the table the letter which she read.
There is no doubt as to the parliamentary rule which requires a minister of the crown who refers to a public document in the house and upon it bases an argument or assertion. That document, if called for, must be produced. The principle involved in such a proceeding is so obvious and reasonable that there does not seem to be any room for argument. It is the principle established in courts of law which prevents counsel from quoting documents which have not been produced in evidence. It has however been held that a demand for production and' filing of any document should be made immediately and not at a subsequent sitting of the house.
There is no standing order which governs the quoting of private communications and we are guided mainly by custom and precedents. I have no doubt in my mind as to the decision I would have rendered with regard to the portion of the letter which the hon. member for North Battleford read into the records on Wednesday last. The contents of that letter are so serious that unless the hon. member, as such member, assumed responsibility for it, then, as Speaker of the house, I would have asked the hon. member to lay the letter on the table of the house or, alternatively, I would have sought the consent of the house that it should be laid on the table. However, the hon. member took the proper course in laying the letter on the table.
It will be noticed that in the letter there is a serious statement concerning an officer of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, one of the departments of government; that it refers specifically to a function of government of a most contentious and delicate character in these war years, namely, the question of internment, and by reason of the publication of the portion of letter in Hansard, it may be properly considered of the nature of a public document. That is all the more reason why it should have been laid on the table and it might have been retained as a parliamentary paper.
It may not be, in other cases of a like nature, so easy to interpret the rules of the
Housing

house. For instance, an unsigned letter should not be read in the house. Mr. Speaker Lemieux so decided on May 16, 1928. Or a member may desire to summarize information contained in a communication, but the member giving the summary must take the responsibility, as a member of this house, for the correctness of the information he or she seeks to give. If an hon. member proposes to read a communication in its entirety, or even a portion, without divulging the name and address of the sender and the member refuses to take the responsibility for the truth and accuracy of the contents, I am clearly of opinion that such a communication should be laid upon the table, and particularly if so desired by any member of the house. In the present case I agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that an hon. member is not entitled to read from communications unless prepared to place them on the table of the house. The principle upon which this is based is that where information is given to the house, the house itself is entitled to the same information as the hon. member who may quote the document.

I have observed in the press a number of dispatches relating to the institution of a large-scale housing project to meet the serious housing shortage existing in certain districts of Canada. This house has not been given any information respecting the government's proposals in this regard. Time and again I have emphasized that when this house is in session announcements of important proposals such as this should be made by the responsible minister in this house rather than communicated directly to the press.
I would ask the minister responsible for the proposed housing programme to give us at once or as soon as reasonably possible a full and detailed statement of the government's plans in this matter.

speechtext:
For some weeks it has become

apparent that in a certain few localities the work of the department is being seriously handicapped by a lack of housing accommodation. In one or two cities it has become utterly impossible to attract the required number of workmen on account of the housing shortage. To meet that situation it has been decided to establish a housing corporation, a wholly owned government company, and Mr. Joseph Pigott has been appointed president of the corporation. Associated with him are six other directors whose names I have not before me at the moment. This corporation has taken over the studies which have been made by officers of the Department of Finance with respect to the housing problem, and it is expected that the corporation will make recommendations to the government shortly as to the best methods of meeting the most urgent situations.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the close of the proceedings last night I stated to the committee that I had dealt with the greater part of what I wished to say with regard to the registration of the human resources of Canada. There were one or two activities with which I did not deal at any length, merely mentioning them, on which I should like to say a few more words to-day.
First, there is the matter of the national registration of the young men who were afterwards called up or are being called up as recruits under the national war services regulations of 1940. Under these regulations, established under the authority of the National Resources Mobilization Act, all male British subjects between the ages of twenty-one and forty-five years inclusive, who are unmarried or widowers without child or children and who have been ordinarily resident in Canada since September 1, 1939, are liable during the continuation of the state of war now existing to be called out for military training for the purpose of the defence and security of Canada. The period of military training and the age class or classes to be called out are determined by proclamation of the governor in council.
For the purpose of calling out men for military training, Canada has been divided into thirteen administrative divisions, corresponding approximately to the military districts of the Department of National Defence. A board of three members, the chairman of which is a judge of the court of the district in which the administrative division is located, is entrusted with the application of the regulations in each administrative division.
The official immediately concerned with the actual calling-out of men is the divisional registrar. Upon receipt of a requisition from the Department of National Defence indicating the number of men required for military
training in each administrative division, divisional registrars proceed to notify men for medical examination who are in the age class or classes rendered subject to call by proclamation. The selection of such men is made proportionately from all parts of the division. Men so notified may report to any duly licensed medical practitioner, which means that any man may go to his family doctor if he so desires. The appointment of all qualified doctors as examining physicians under the regulations was decided upon after consulting with the Canadian Medical Association. May I say here that the medical profession of Canada has responded whole-heartedly to this call for national service and that the examining physicians have performed their duties conscientiously and efficiently.
In order to obtain the number of men required to attend the several military training centres of the Department of National Defence, it is necessary for the divisional registrars to notify a number substantially larger than the one called for, in order to take care of those who are categorized as temporarily and permanently unfit for military training, and also of those who, for reasons of seasonal occupations or essential employment in war industries, cannot be called out for a particular period of training. For the first three periods of military training, the number of men categorized lower than C. 1 averaged 23-1 per cent of the total number of men called out for medical examination. This ratio is well within the percentage of medical rejections to be normally expected in such a large scale medical examination.
I recall that in the discussion which took place in the house a few days ago it was indicated that a considerable number of the men who did report to camp were afterwards found to be not physically fit, a larger number than probably would have been expected had we had some experience in matters of this kind.
The second step in bringing men to the training centres is to select from the thousands of medical reports received from the examining physicians in each administrative division the men who come within the medical categories accepted for training by the Department of National Defence. The men selected are then notified by the divisional registrar to report, on a stated date, to the officer commanding a stated training centre.

The divisional registrar encloses with the "notice-military training" warrants for trans-portatien, meals, and/or lodging as may be required. Upon arriving at the training centre the men are again examined by the military doctors and, if found medically fit, are accepted for military training. From the moment they are accepted at the military training centre, the men cease to be under the jurisdiction of the Department of National War Services, because they are enrolled in the reserve of the' Canadian army.
It is important that this should be understood. because continuously we have inquiries from hon. members and others with regard to matters which really come under the Department of National Defence. The men are more or less under the Department of National War Services from the time the call goes *>ut to them to report to the physician, until such time as they have been accepted in a military training camp; from that time on, they are under the control of the Department of National Defence.
That, I think, is all that it is necessary for me to say with regard to the activities of the Department of National War Services in connection with the calling up of men. Any questions which hon. members may have with regard to costs and all matters of that kind can be dealt with when we are in committee on the amounts estimated as necessary during the coming year.

One other matter to which I wish to refer, and which is under the Department of National War Services, has to do with voluntary services. It will be recalled that when the department was set up there were five organizations which were doing auxiliary work for the Department of National Defence, and it was stated at that time that instead of having five different appeals for funds made to the people of Canada, attempts should be made to have these appeals made all at one time and in one organized effort. At the time it was suggested this should be done, some of these organizations had already set out to make their appeal to the public, that was at the end of last year. One of them, the Red Cross, had gone so far with their preparations that it was not thought wise then to attempt, in the short time left, to get these organizations all working together in a common effort, and it was finally decided that the Red Cross should go ahead with their drive. Later on, it was thought wise that the other organizations should combine in one drive in the spring of this year, and that has been arranged for the 24th of March next.
I should like to give the committee an outline of the activities in that regard up to the moment.
Administration of the War Charities Act. The object of this act is to provide a measure of control and regulation of the voluntary efforts of organizations throughout Canada, in their desire to raise money for war and charitable purposes. Any organization which makes an appeal to the public for donations or subscriptions in money or in kind, or any war charity fund which attempts to do so by sponsoring a bazaar or any other entertainment for that purpose, must be registered

War Appropriation Bill
under the act. From the time the act was assented to on September 13, 1939, up to February 25, 1941, some 907 central funds have been so registered. In addition to these, 739 branch funds have been registered under the central fund. This means, for example, that the national Imperial Order Daughters of the Empire, is registered as a central fund, and many of its branches are also registered. The great majority of applications come from responsible groups or organizations. Upon investigation, certificates are issued to such organizations. Unfortunately some of the applications come from individuals or groups whose main object seems to be to gain some advantage-perhaps it is a financial one-by doing a certain job, possibly in a good way, but with the result that too great a part of the funds will go to an individual rather than to the charity. Such applications, after investigation, are refused. Every effort has been made to prevent the commercializing of war charity efforts. In a few instances it has been necessary to cancel the registration of organizations because their work was unsatisfactory in that regard.
We are trying to show organizations that in planning their work great care should be exercised so that the cost of raising funds may be kept to the minimum. The national war charities funds advisory board, under the chairmanship of Mr. C. L. Burton, was set up, and it is rendering a service to the country by checking up the budgets of the larger organizations that make application for the right to collect funds, and by passing on advice to myself as minister, and) through the minister to the government, as to what is thought advisable in connection with funds of that kind.
Investigations of that sort have been carried on in relation to the drive which will start on March 24 next, and five of the larger organizations have united in order to make a combined appeal to the people of Canada for $5,500,000. They are going out to make that appeal with the endorsation of the government, and the government has, through
them,	made an appeal to the people to support these efforts in view of their relationship to the general war effort.

There is one other matter which I mentioned last night to which I wish to return this afternoon. It has to do with what is known as the information bureau. Probably before dealing with one or two matters in particular I should give to the committee some idea of the organization of the information bureau. I believe it has already been indicated in answer to questions in the house that the organization was first set up by order in council P.C. 4073 on December 8, 1939. On January 3, 1940, Mr. Thompson, who was the first director of public information, was forced by ill health to resign. Mr. G. H. Lash, of Montreal, Mr. Thompson's assistant, was appointed acting director and since that time he has been made director. On February 23 there was appointed as a director Mr. Claude Melancon, previously joint press censor for Canada. On July 19 the office of the director of public information was transferred to the Department of National War Services and since then has been operated under this department. There has been some discussion in the house since the opening of the session, and in the press before the opening, as to the activities of this bureau in connection with press releases. I merely want to make the practice known so that hon. members will all be familiar with the facts in discussing matters having to do with it.
In the first place, after careful consideration of the whole matter with representatives of the press and with those who are prominent in the press association across Canada, and after consultation with many who had had previous experience in connection with the matter, it was decided not to attempt to appoint under this bureau a publicity agent who would gather together all the information obtainable from different departments of government and hand that out as one piece of information to the press of Canada. Certain reasons were put forward why that should not be done, one being that the representatives of the press could gain that information in Ottawa as readily as any individual could gather it for them; and with a score or more of representatives of the press gathering information around Ottawa and expressing their views through their own papers, the public were more likely to get the type of information which they ought to get while we are conducting a war, or under any other circumstances. Whether that is the correct procedure to follow or not, it is the procedure which has been followed up to the
present time. The papers all have their representatives in Ottawa, as they have in the press gallery at this moment; they can get whatever information is available, and as a result of obtaining that information, I assume they write their articles.
It was arranged that in order to expedite their efforts to get information we should have as many ministerial press conferences as possible. When the press is anxious to have them we try to arrange them, and when ministers have something in particular to give out they arrange for a press conference. As a matter of fact, the ministries concerned with war effort decided upon certain days that they would be prepared to meet the press if the press desired to meet them and discuss with them matters having to do with war services.
That, generally speaking, is the method by which the information is given out to the press. In addition to that, there are in the different departments of government, more particularly in the war services department, information organizations or publicity organizations, which from time to time issue statements having to do with the affairs of their particular departments. Those statements do not always go directly to the press, although some may do so. The greater part of them go to the bureau of information. All the bureau of information does with press releases from the different departments is to mail them to wherever they are intended to go. That is, we do not edit them; we do not change anything that is in them; we simply take them as they come to us and send them out. In other words, the only responsibility in connection with the distribution of press releases of that kind, that can be charged up to the fund which we are -now discussing in relation to the war services department, is the cost of distribution, and nothing more. The work of writing and compiling of them is all done in the other departments.
In addition to that, we may put out some press releases, but practically all of the press releases which are put out by the department itself simply give background; that is, they are not intended to go into to-morrow's daily paper as news, but are intended to give the editorial writer or anyone in the newspaper office information to which he can go at any time and obtain what were presumed to be the facts at the time when this particular information was sent out. Or it may be that it covers a period of time about which there has been some discussion over the country, and information is sent in order to indicate what may have been the facts in connection with it. It is not always used in the press, but, I assume, is put away on files to be referred to from time to time as needed.

That explains largely what is being done by the information bureau in relation to press releases.
In addition to that, we have illustrated material. I should like to read to the committee some particulars regarding the sending out of illustrated material.
The photographic branch of public information was not established until May 1, 1940, that is less than a year ago. From then until January 31, 1941, the branch has distributed 75,714 pieces of illustrated material, as follows:

Do hon. members know how this editor arrived at the amount of $262? He took the 772 press releases and divided that number into $202,672, the amount spent for all the radio activity, all the motion picture work, all the posters to which I referred, all the pamphlets that were sent out and everything done by the information bureau; these were all made charges against the press releases, and it was stated that these cost $262 each. The $202,672 paid out of the national treasury for government propaganda is roughly twice the combined salaries of the forty correspondents who cover the proceedings of parliament for the press of Canada.
I would hope that was so, because all the activities associated with the bureau, including those I have outlined, are covered by that $202,000.

This editor states what is obviously incorrect, if not untrue-and I distinguish between the two terms because I cannot understand any newspaper as prominent as the Toronto Globe and Mail having an editor who could not read that return and understand it. I suggest that it would appear to be an intentional misrepresentation. At a time when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) was appealing to the people of Canada for subscriptions in connection with his drive for funds, this paper tells the people that one of the departments of government spent $202,000 on 772 press releases, or $262 per press release. If the taxpayers had the faintest conception of how their money is poured down a dozen different sewers on parliament hill there would be a rebellion.
I do not think that we have to take advice from the Toronto Globe and Mail about money being poured down sewers. The Toronto Globe and Mail used to be published in a building which suited its purposes very well, but one has only to go and look at the building in which it is published to-day to understand how they pour money down the sewer. For an organization of that kind to be criticizing, even though their criticism were right, is I think drawing the long bow in connection with matters of this kind.

The word "propaganda" has been given different meanings. Used in the best sense of the term, propaganda is, as I think every hon. member will agree, worth while; that is, propaganda based upon facts. The efforts of the bureau in the matter of publications may properly be termed propaganda if the putting-out of a picture indicating, for example, exactly what is being done in some part of the empire or in Canada can be termed propaganda. Radio broadcasts- it may be fiction; nevertheless fiction that illustrates something that is actually going on-I would also consider legitimate propaganda, and something which is not only legitimate but really ought to be done.
I would not altogether agree with the hon. member who suggested last night-it may not be the same member as the one to whom the leader of the opposition just referred- that we needed a ministry of enlightenment. The conclusion I have arrived at after serving for twenty-seven years either in the legislature or in the House of Commons, is that if you want to be enlightened you must enlighten yourself. There are a great many sources from which you can get information, but I do not think any ministry of any kind could really enlighten the people in general because they must get the information and then study it and arrive at their own conclusions as a result of their studies.

speechtext:
May I draw to the attention of the committee a matter which has assumed considerable importance in our part of the dominion, particularly in Ontario? I raise this question at the moment because the Minister of National War Services has under his jurisdiction a division which has to do with material resources in connection with our war effort. My conception of the department over which he has control and jurisdiction is that, to some extent in any event, there shall be planning in a systematic way in respect of our war effort. I realize every difficulty with which he is confronted, and I am sympathetic with him in that regard. But so far as our material resources are concerned and the plans which are being effectuated for the national mobilization of industry as it fits into our war effort, I believe the matter about which I am going to speak deserves immediate and special consideration.
On the 1st of March, the farming population of Ontario received a considerable shock when they heard that the Ontario agricultural college, one of the centres of agricultural technical and practical training, was to be closed and that the premises would be occupied by No. 4 wireless school of the empire air training scheme. In justice to the agricultural population, many of whom I represent, I ought to make it clear that I have not heard one farmer suggest that anything he can give or any action whereby he can cooperate should not be freely given to the cause of Canada and the empire. When I raise my voice in
War Appropriation Bill

connection with this matter I want to make it abundantly clear that the attitude of the farmer in this matter is not based on any narrow ideas as to his own particular future.
May I, however, point out to the minister that we have now been at war for something like eighteen months, a time sufficient, surely, to give the government some opportunity to plan our effort on comprehensive lines. The government may fairly be forgiven for whatever mistakes were made when the war first broke out and during the cataclysm which followed shortly afterwards. After all, this government is as human, or perhaps almost as human as the rest of us; at any rate it should receive that degree of consideration. But when plans are being laid for the continued prosecution of our war effort, it seems important that, in taking over buildings for these purposes, care should be exercised that peace-time institutions are transformed to war-time uses, not that war-time institutions are changed to other types of war-time endeavour, because I believe I voice the opinion of many agriculturists and others when I say that part and parcel of Canada's war effort is the production of foodstuffs and the extension of educational and technical advantages in so far as that production is concerned. It is along that line that I wish to bring this matter to the attention of the government.
It has been suggested in some newspapers- although, as the Minister of National War Services has said, their information may be wrong-that it is doubtful whether the officers of the Department of National Defence were wholly in agreement with the taking over of Guelph agricultural college for No. 4 wireless training school. I am in no position to say whether that is so; but in any event it seems to me that, with 600 male students and 200 female students at the college, and a large staff, built up in a selective way, of some of the best agricultural experts in Canada to-day, the institution should not be suddenly disbanded in order that another type of wartime activity may take its place unless it is absolutely essential to our war effort.
If it is a fact that No. 4 wireless training school can find no more suitable place, or no place equally suitable, there will not be from me the slightest complaint about the taking over of the building. If, however, there be any possible substitute, it seems to me that the present choice shows a lamentable lack of planning. If we ever needed a plan so far as our general war-time activity is concerned, now is the time to start it if it has not been started before.
Further, it is my recollection-and I have been on that model farm many times-that the property includes nearly 800 acres devoted

to experimental purposes. Those experiments have been carried on at great cost, and farmers all over Canada, particularly Ontario, are very much interested in the work going on.

I am glad to hear the acting minister of agriculture make that remark. I accept his statement, and I urge that the benefits of this experimentation be not lost to agriculture at this' time. As a matter of fact, so far as I know, there has not been any definite official statement as to the carrying-on of these experiments. Whatever is done, whether or not any change is made in the plan for the use of the college, we must not deprive the farmers of Canada of the technical advantages which they are enjoying as a result of these experimental activities.
When this war is over and the period of rehabilitation begins, it will cost much money and take a great deal of time to put these technical experiments in agriculture back where they were before. I am trying to emphasize to the minister, in all fairness, that, if there be any other way of providing for the wireless training school, whereby the empire air training plan will not be hampered or hindered, I trust he will use his influence to leave in operation our agricultural college at Guelph.
We talk a good deal in this chamber about agriculture, but it must be realized that, in so far as the interests of the farmers are concerned, the county agricultural representatives who get much of their information and practically all of their early training from the agricultural college at Guelph are able to render a tremendous service to the people of the province. They have technical, theoretical and practical experience. I wish to say a word this afternoon on their behalf. If the proposed change is absolutely necessary for the prosecution of our war effort, I am all for it, regardless of the consequences. May I, however, ask the minister to see whether a plan cannot be adopted so that we shall be able, as far as possible, to avoid changing from one important war-time industry to another, but rather so that the peace-time industries of the country may first be converted into and form a part of our integrated war effort before those which are already in war work. I make this appeal to the minister on behalf of agriculture, not by way of carping criticism of the government, because I have every sympathy with them in their difficulties; but it would be regarded as a good move on behalf of the agricultural communities who are struggling to-day if their college facilities

War Appropriation Bill
could be restored without in any way injuring or hampering or interfering with the general war effort of the nation.

In answer to what has
been said by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), the premier of Ontario should be praised for having the Guelph agricultural college used as a school for training for war purposes, and since they are apparently so zealous in their war aims, I do not see why Conservative members are critical about the matter. I live in a district in which there are many farmers. Many of them have been attending agricultural schools and- have been doing very well, but they understand- that during the war it is right to make sacrifices in order to defend the country.
I must say that I do not feel very comfortable about what I said yesterday when the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Mac-Nicol) was speaking. I interjected some remarks in the middle of his speech and since then I have read his speech in extenso and found it a m-ost interesting one. Turning to page 1141 of Hansard of Friday last, I note what was said- by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) about bringing back that great windbag the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. There is probably no one in the house who was more intimate in using him as a punching bag when he was prime minister and also leader of the opposition. He was a complete failure from every point of view, so much so that the Conservative party vomited him, and I d-o not see why they want to have him back. I am sorry to say that, but I must give an exact description of what happened when the right hon. gentleman was leader of his party, when he was called- humbug by Mr. Thomas in England, and so on. We had enough of him. Besides, he wanted to leave us, and he has gone. Let him be alone and happy. But he was a failure as head of his party and as head of his government, and I d-o not see what use he would be here during the war. The joke of it is here:
I suggest that, with a view to preventing the possibility of failures such as have occurred in the last six months in the matter of aircraft production, we have set up at this time a committee composed of representatives of the aircraft industry in Canada, and that we get in touch with the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, acquainted as he is with requirements in Great Britain, and experienced as he must be in consequence of the assistance he has given Lord Beaverbrook, -and have him come to Canada and head a committee or, if you like, a commission, to investigate the whole situation with regard to the failure of our aircraft production. to the end that further failures will not have to be admitted in this chamber.
The word "failures" is repeated several times, probably in order to describe Mr. Bennett himself. But I do not see how failure can -be prevented by bringing another failure to Canada. My hon. friend the member for Lake Centre is too bright a member to continue along such a line. He must change his mind, and he must remember also that not only did the Tory party reject Mr. Bennett but that when he left Ottawa there were only two or three members of the party, one of whom has died, to accompany him to the station. Mr. Bennett was so sorry about it that he shed tears on that occasion. We do not need him any more, and that is the opinion not only of the member for Temiscouata. It is the general opinion in Canada. The Canadian people do not want him. My hon. friends are most illogical. The people of Canada gave a large majority to the King government at the last election, and yet my hon. friends say that this government has no mandate from the people. What mandate has Mr. Bennett now since leaving?-and he left after he was defeated. He had only a handful of followers and they changed him for another leader and again changed that other leader, so that now they have a temporary leader. I do not know how long he will keep that seat.
But coming to that very gentleman, the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) I want to go back a little further to page 903 of Hansard, of February 21, when he tried to give me a lecture. I will stand for no lecture from the leader of the opposition. I will not refer to a dead speaker but to one of the previous speakers to witness the fact that I have no lesson in dignity to learn from the present leader of the opposition. The best way for him to preach dignity is by example. There is something else I find in Hansard at page 901, where the word "vicious" is added to the remarks of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). When he spoke in answer to me he said that I had made an attack upon him. That was his view. Afterwards, when I read Hansard, I saw that the word "vicious" was added in pencil, and I do not know whether it was done by Major Leighton, who is n-ow press liaison officer of his department, formerly managing editor of a Ku Klux paper and also former editor of the Bennett Regina Star, which is dead now. I find it unbelievable to discover unparliamentary words in Hansard when they have not been uttered in the house, and I would make a suggestion in virtue of which all members would be equal. It is that the corrections in Hansard be made in the house at the opening of the afternoon sitting, and then people would know what the report is
War Appropriation Bill

that we have before us, and there would be no possibility of change. I have seen one member redrafting whole pages in his own handwriting, like a boy's composition. It is absurd. What is said in the house is what people would know. They are not interested in academic write-ups but what is said in the house, and if a correction has to be made it is very easy for a member to bring it up at the beginning of the sitting. Then people would have a true picture of what had taken place, and if there were something wrong then members could do what I have done with regard to the hon. member for Davenport- express regret.' But people would have the real picture, and Hansard would not be like the mirrors we see in fairs. If the mirror is on the side the man looks wide, if he looks on the other side he is just as high-he is a giant. It is a farce, and it seems to me that if we are to have Hansard it must be true and accurate. If people have the liberty to change anything they say in Hansard and put unparliamentary words in their speeches when they are afraid to use them in the house it is just as well to stop Hansard.
There was something else said, and on that I congratulate the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I complained about some foolish expenditure that was made at St. Paul l'Ermite. I have learned with satisfaction that after these remarks were made in the house about fifty men were suspended at that place. This is the way things should be done. That the matter was not brought up by the leader of the opposition is probably because they are milk brothers of R. B. Bennett who are heads of the concern operating at that point, and he wanted to protect the Tories there. He was afraid of them, and I know that the leader of the opposition will never bring up a thing like that because he would expose his own friends. The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Fleming) yesterday said something which was absolutely true; he said that by the appointment of Tories-not all of them, but some of them-in responsible and strategic positions the Liberal party is suffering from their extravagance and foolishness. If I denounced it at times it is not only to defend my party, it is to prevent foolish expenditure. We have every right to get all the information about it.
There is a difference between strategic information and information on expenditure. My contention is that we should have all information about expenditure; nothing should be secret. Of course if one looks at the estimates we find there the job and the salary, but without any name. If we look at another book, the report of the auditor general, there is the name of the civil servant and the salary, 
but no mention of the job, except in a very few cases. Then in the departmental report everything is anonymous except the deputy minister who submits the report to the minister; there is no name, no job and no salary mentioned. Of course the branches are mentioned, but I do not see them mentioned in the report of the auditor general except in a very few cases.
Now we have this war appropriation bill. It is not only during the war that we have the Department of National Defence; we have it also in times of peace. During that time the whole thing was in the main estimates; now we have nothing in the main estimates for the Department of National Defence, the Department of National Defence for Air and the Department of Munitions and Supply. All the names and jobs and salaries of everyone employed here in Ottawa in any department should be there; whether the functions of those departments are temporary or not does not matter. We have to render account of the moneys expended by the treasury and therefore must be in a position to give all information to our constituents when they ask for it. That seems only reasonable.
This year the report of the auditor general is entirely different in form from what it was in other years. There are important amounts of money that are not mentioned. I do not know where we should go to get information on them. Yet when any elector comes to see an hon. member and asks him about the expenditure for the salary of so and so, if we do not find it in the report of the auditor general where can we find it?
Besides that the government complain they have to answer too many questions about salaries. It is their own fault; we should have that information in the proper place. One may say it would mean a certain expenditure for printing. It is the old excuse given to me by Mr. Dunning when he refused to print the report of the civil service committee. I had to fight with him to get the report printed and afterwards there was no reprint.
Now I bring to the attention especially of the Prime Minister and his colleagues this report of the auditor general for the year ended March 31, 1940. It is most incomplete; it is worthless. Every cent of expenditure should be shown in it. They say a few dollars are saved by not printing all salaries in full. It is the first time in my long career as a parliamentarian that it has happened and I denounce it. The auditor general should be very careful. I had something to say about him some years ago and I was stopped. I

War Appropriation Bill
could tell the whole story-the trouble that was then made about a messenger who was employed here and who had been recommended by me. Someone tried to make him suffer because I complained about certain people. The auditor general should be censured by this house for not giving us full information about expenditures in all departments. The ministers have no reason to complain that there are questions about salaries and expenditures; we cannot get the information in the proper place. I am sure that by mentioning that I express the views of a large number of Liberal members and members belonging to other groups.
The appropriations or estimates for the headquarters of all war departments should be in the main estimates, including not only mention of the job and the salary but the name of the individual. It would not cost so much to do that. To try to find some information we have to look at the report of the auditor general, which does not contain complete information, and we have to look at the estimate. In the report of the department there is nothing about what is paid the various individuals. That report should mean something, but it is an example of the vague information that I complained of some time ago. We have a great deal of paper but we cannot find anything in it; everything is mixed up-it is like a waste-paper basket. It is not worthy of the House of Commons and the parliament of Canada.
The estimates should contain information about the headquarters staff for each war department and staff salaries. Speaking of staff, I mean everyone from the deputy minister to the last appointed stenographer, mentioning the name, position, salary and allowances paid to each. If that were done it would facilitate the work of the war expenditures committee.
But there is something else. It is the fact that here in Ottawa the staff is part civilian and part military. The men are military and the women civilian. It seems strange at times; I do not see why a clerk whose duty is to file papers, or a messenger whose duty is to carry letters from pillar to post should wear a uniform and be entitled to allowances besides his salary. Of course there is a certain snobbery in that. During the war it is a consideration to wear a uniform, even if one is not doing any military duty. Many men are wearing uniforms who are not fit for military duty. For instance, here I have a list of the ranks in the air department. It starts with pilot officer, then goes on to flying officer, flight lieutenant, squadron leader, wing commander, group captain, air commodore, air vice marshal, air marshal, air chief marshal and marshal of the Royal Air Force. There are some pilot officers who are only piloting files, some flying officers who only fly to the door to take the salute; and I could continue at great length. On the other hand we have a girl, a stenographer, who hears very confidential information but who is in civilian clothes, buying her dress at Murphy Gamble's or some other store. There is nothing military about her. The other man is in uniform, and in addition to his salary he is paid an allowance about which we do not know, although both do the very same work. These are foolish expenditures, and the ministers concerned should bring these fellows to their senses. I do not see why a man should wear a uniform when he is performing duties that were performed yesterday by a young girl in civilian clothes, duties which might be performed to-morrow by that same young girl. This is not the army at all; this is just a parade, which is absurd in times like these.
The other day I suggested that the government should look into the expenditures at St. Paul l'Ermite, and I also mention Valley-field, where the expenditure, which was supposed to be $5,000, has gone to $16,000 or $25,000, or some very high figure. I hope the ministers concerned will get in touch with the proper authorities in order that some investigation may be made. Moreover, investigation should be made into the qualifications of the inspectors. I know of one leather inspector in the Department of National Defence who was formerly a truck driver, and in addition I believe he is an Italian, a spaghetti eater. Another inspector was in a hospital for a time performing the duties of a he-nurse; then he was a packer and now he is a leather inspector receiving a salary and a living allowance. I am told that very few of the leather inspectors were previously qualified as saddlers, harness makers or leather workers. If we want our money to be well spent we must have duly qualified inspectors rather than men appointed because of their friendship with a great man, though friendship with a great man is a godly thing.
As another suggestion, I want the government to be very careful about soldiers travelling on trains, to see that they are not given an opportunity to buy hard liquor when on ordinary passenger trains. I might mention some instances that were very bad. One night the maritime express arrived in Montreal with one car full of soldiers. All the windows of that car were broken. On another occasion the conductor complained of the way some soldiers had behaved. When he went into
War Appropriation Bill

the car the lights were all out. He turned the lights ou again and told the soldiers to leave them on. When he returned later all the lights had been unscrewed and thrown away, and the car was as dark as a cave. These things have been passed over in silence for a long .time, but a stop should be put to conduct of this kind. Of course some officers- I do not know of what branch-are supposed to be on the trains to police the oars, but what I have mentioned should be stopped in order that the Canadian people may retain their high regard for the army. There are times when soldiers can have a drink without jausing any trouble. I do not wish to cast any slur on the army; when young men are left without control this sort of thing is bound to happen. I am all for order in the army; I am for .the hierarchy, but we know very well that the hierarchy cannot work from side to side, that it works from top to bottom.
I could make reference to many other matters, but I shall conclude by mentioning only one. Bach of us realizes that war is a most serious thing and that probably we will have to stand by our soldiers, our sailors and our airmen for more than a year or two before we reach the turning .point and achieve victory. We are told that many sacrifices are ahead; but there is one class of preacher to which I object. I have before me a dispatch that appeared in the Ottawa Journal of December 12, 1940, as follows:
Canada Urged to Reduce Home Consumption. otoke-On-Trent, Staffordshire, England. December 11. Canada and the other dominions are urged by Lord Stamp to join with the United Kingdom in tightening their belts and reducing home consumption so that the war effort may be increased to the utmost peak.
That was none of his business. He may speak to Englishmen, but we have no lesson to learn from Lord Stamp. Members of the government may speak to us, but it does not help our cause for a man in England to tell us to tighten our belts. That is our own business; it is none of his. These speeches are very dangerous; they may arouse the Canadian people.
There is one other matter, Mr. Speaker. Everyone in this country wants to know what protection we are getting as a result of the expenditures that are being made. We hear of billions of dollars being spent for Canada. We may see trains loaded with shells. We may see trainloads of soldiers. We are ready to vote all the money necessary to win the war. That is right; everyone is for that, but we want that money to give a certain definite amount of protection to the Canadian people. Of course there are two schools of thought on that point. There is the school 
that believes everything should be sent to Great Britain, overlooking the defence of Canada. There is the other school that does not want to d.o anything for Great Britain but wants all the war expenditures to be made for the benefit of Canada. I believe it is best to follow the middle course. We must help Great Britain as much as we can; but we must not overlook the defence of our own country. While the Prime Minister did not accept my suggestion, I suggested that every hon. member should go to his constituency and recruit a full battalion, a thousand or twelve hundred men, from the day labourers, the farm hands and the lumber jacks-the very best type of soldiers-who would enlist for the defence of Canada. At that time it was not accepted.
It seems that we should try to restore the confidence of the Canadian people in the ministry by seeing that the country is well defended. St. Martin was a very charitable man. When he was asked for some help by a poor man he cut his -cloak in half, gave him one-half and kept the other half for himself. But he did not give his underwear. In these times there is no one who admires Churchill more than I do, but I do not place Lord Beaverbrook upon the same pedestal. That is my own point of view and it is just as reasonable as the views put out by those paid by him to say that he is a great man. And Lord Stamp comes to this country to give us a lesson, I have a perfect right to tell him my views.
If we are to help England, let us do so, but let us at the same time defend Canada. We should organize our defence in case of the sudden attack which may come at any time. We do not know what may happen in the future. We hope that the future will be bright; that is the hope of everyone, but we must protect ourselves. I hope that in the money included in this vote there will be a large amount provided to organize the defence of Canada. We need to 'be defended, because we are a large country with a small population. We are, as the Prime Minister has said repeatedly, envied by many countries in Europe. We must be ready to repulse any attack.
When the government takes that fact into consideration and acts accordingly it will find out that the Canadian people are satisfied and ready to do more than ever for England. But first let us organize the defence of Canada. The Minister of National Defence and the other war ministers will be surprised at the extent to which I am ready to help, provided that they take the members into their confidence and do not treat them as strangers. If they are occupying the treasury benches, it is not by

W ar Appropriation Bill
a mandate of God but by the will of each member who supports the government. That should not be forgotten; that is something that deserves consideration and I hope it will not be ignored.
The press which is paid by the profiteers who are the scum of the world can say anything. I dio not care about that. The press has lost a lot of influence by using stupid language about some important matters. Very few people read the editorial pages of a paper. When they want to know the news they listen to the radio. They are not interested in the papers except to make parcels with them.
In conclusion I insist upon the defence of this country and I hope it will not be forgotten by those whom it may concern.

I should like to make a few remarks with reference to the statement made by the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner) and to ask him a question or two.
First, I think the minister should be commended for the work being done by the bureau of public information.	I am not
suggesting for a moment that that work cannot be improved, and I do not think the minister would suggest that. This is a new branch. To organize the propaganda-I use that word advisedly in its proper sense-of a nation in a few short months is a herculean task. Some of the work being done in this connection is extremely commendable. I think all hon. members who have listened to the series "Let's Face the Facts" will agree with me when I say that that was one of the finest series ever put on the air. I have heard many persons who are in a position to know say that the address by Hendrik Van Loon was a classic, probably one of the greatest things ever sent over the ether waves. The same is true of many other radio programmes. I think they have done most excellent work.
The posters and pictures put out have had a very telling effect right across Canada. I should like to pay a tribute to the work done by the national film board. I am sure that most hon. members saw the picture at the Capitol theatre a week ago yesterday. I went to another picture theatre a few nights later when the same picture was shown and I tried to get the public reaction from the audience. Everywhere this picture is being shown it receives the most satisfactory ovation. I doubt if the people who put out the March of Time and who received an award for it could have done a better job. I hope that whoever is responsible for this type of work in the department will be kept at it. By having pictures like this shown in the theatres across Canada we help to build up public morale. I doubt if public morale can be built
up as adequately in any other way. The radio and the moving pictures are important media for this purpose, and I think the minister is making fairly good use of them.
As I say, I am not suggesting that this work cannot be improved. For instance, the minister has said that the material sent out by the director of public information is sent out just as it is received from the different departments. I think that is what is wrong with it. It would be much better if some newspaper man in the bureau wrote it over again in the style which newspaper men know the public considers readable. A lot of this information could be rehashed and condensed. There is such an avalanche of it that a lot of it does find its way into the waste-paper basket. It could be boiled down; many of the statistics could be eliminated and the interesting facts put into the leading paragraphs.
Hon. members appreciate the thanks expressed by the minister for the part they took in the national registration last year. I believe all hon. members cooperated to the best of their ability. But I should like to say this to the minister, and I say it in the best spirit:	Last year the minister wanted a
national registration and he wanted it quickly, so he called upon hon. members and asked them to give of their time and services. They did that gladly and willingly and the registration was a success; indeed it is a monument to the way in which public men can cooperate when they want to. In every constituency where I had the privilege of looking into the organization work I found people of all political faiths and religious beliefs cooperating; they were freely giving their services and giving them gladly. The result is that that registration cost less than a million dollars.
Now the minister has started a salvage campaign and the members are again being asked to give of their time and services. They are doing it gladly. They are endeavouring to show how they can be of service to the country and to the minister who is responsible for this work. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) wanted cooperation in connection with the war savings certificate drive, and I think he got it from all hon. members. But this is how the picture looks to some people in the country. They say: When you wanted a national registration, you came and asked for a voluntary effort; when you wanted to conduct a salvage campaign, you asked for a voluntary effort; when you wanted assistance in the war service certificate campaign you asked for a voluntary effort, but now when you are going to take the census, which will cost in the neighbourhood of $2,500,000-the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. War Appropriation Bill

MacKinnon) will know-when there is some money to be expended, the work is being done on a partisan basis. The Minister of Trade and Commerce shakes his head, but I am not going to get into an argument with him about it. Every question which has appeared on the order paper in connection with the census commissioners who have been appointed shows clearly that this is being done on a partisan basis.
I know that no hon. members on this side of the house have been consulted with reference to the carrying on of the census. Since . we have been doing these other things so successfully on a voluntary basis, I think the minister might well consider the advisability of taking the census, if it is to be proceeded with at all-and that is debatable-on the same basis as the national registration was taken. It could be done that way for very much less money. The minister would have the cooperation of members in all parts of the house, and it would help the people throughout the country who gave their voluntary services last year to feel that they were not merely being used in a pinch and then cast aside when they might have an opportunity to receive something for their services. I throw that out as a suggestion for the minister because I am sure that it will not be as easy to get the voluntary cooperation of these people again if we drop this precedent we established in connection with national registration and have the census taken purely on a partisan basis, as it would appear it is going to be taken.
I have a question to ask of the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner). I understand that there are no estimates for his department unless they are brought down in the supplementaries, and that consequently this is the only opportunity we shall have to get a picture of the expenditures of the department for the past year and an outline of the budget for the coming year. I would therefore ask the minister if he will be kind enough to break down the expenditures of his department for the past year up to the most recent date available. I should like to know the total amount spent by his department during the past year and what will be spent this year.
We have the item of $918,000 for the registration. I should also like to know the total amount that was spent in calling up the trainees for training and the total amount that was spent in organizing the voluntary services. The minister has already given us the amount spent by the information bureau up to the end of November. Could we have the expenditure brought up to the latest date available? I would also ask the minister to

break down these expenditures into their component parts and to give us the corresponding amounts that will be spent for the same purposes in the coming year. If the minister would give us these items now, it would be helpful.
With reference to the trainees, when the Minister of National War Services has finished would the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) give us, if not now, at all events later, what it costs the country for the pay of the trainees, their equipment, the training facilities required in their thirty days' training, the cost of the medical examinations, et cetera.
