speechtext:
Those
expenditures and estimates should be laid on the table in printed form so that we can have an opportunity to study them.
While I am on my feet I should like to say this. At the last session of parliament we were asked to vote a war appropriation of $700,000,000, the details of which expenditure are presently under review. We facilitated the passage of that resolution as no other resolution was ever facilitated in the whole history of the House of Commons, and when I hear hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches criticize us for what they consider to be destructive criticism under this measure they are entirely oblivious of the fact that we facilitated the passage of that other resolution to help the war effort and with hardly a word of information about it. That is just in passing.
In that same session of parliament, because of the tragedy of the events then occurring and because of the nature of the times, we did not ask, except in a brief and very general way, as to the war credit that had been voted at the preceding session of parliament. Was that not cooperation? It was cooperation of a kind that I do not think ought ever to occur in parliament again, and I promise the ministry that as long as I am at this desk that sort of thing will not occur again. The people of Canada want to know, and they never can know unless the government give us some detailed information in advance for study. The ministry must have anticipated, when this Sl,300,000,000 appropriation measure was brought down, that there would be discussion and that naturally we would want information. The Minister of National War Services himself, in the course of his statement, made it clear that he anticipated that we would ask and would receive the break-down of all the expenditures in his department. How can any opposition, no matter what its desire may be, ask intelligent questions about any department of war expenditures unless we have placed in front of us some picture that we can study?
With respect to the question of the thirty-day training I got a certain number of figures from the Minister of National Defence and a number of figures from the Minister of National War Services, but they are by no means complete. As the opportunity arises, I propose to ask to have them broken down, but I did not want to bring that up this afternoon because my colleague wants to ask the
Minister of Munitions and Supply about another matter, and I do not wish to occupy his place too long because his question is important.
I am making a plea now for the ministry to take into consideration over the week-end breaking down by departments, and under suitable and proper headings, every dollar of the $1,300,000,000 that they are asking for now, save and except such as they say are secret, and I certainly shall never ask for that. I am prepared to take the word of the minister that they are secret and that details cannot be published. But with respect to those that are not secret with respect to those on which it is our duty to the country to get information, I do ask the ministry, and it ought to have been done by the Minister of Finance quite a while ago as soon as he brought down his appropriation, that we be given the information for which I have asked. I know that we have been given general figures which are on Hansard, but we have not been supplied with a printed statement showing the expenditures by the various departments and under proper headings. I should like to have that information, broken down as far as would be reasonably necessary for intelligent examination and discussion. I do plead with the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of National War Services and all the other ministers who are spending this huge sum of money to give this information to the house and the country. I do not think it is very difficult. If the Minister of National War Services were to allow me to see that portfolio in front of him, I venture to say it contains a breakdown of every dollar of proposed expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I will give it if the hon. member will let me.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Why cannot we get it in the form of a pamphlet? It would involve only the cost of the printing. I asked the other day, in addition to the figures that were given, for the cost of transportation of the trainees to the camp. That is an important item. It goes into the cost of training these young men. It is part and parcel of the equity we have in these young men for future war services in Canada. That has not been given to us yet, and it is over a week since we asked for those figures. I communicated with the deputy minister; he told me they were not available. I cannot quite understand that. These men were called up first in October. The transportation cost must have been heavy. All the bills for the October camp, for taking the men home, and for bringing up the next group must have been submitted and paid before the end of
War Appropriation Bill

the year. I should like to get that information. I should like to get the cost for the January camp and, as far as possible, down to date. I want the total cost of the thirty-day training plan. I believe that when the house and the country get the figures on this plan they will be astonished at the cost.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: How much does the hon. member think it will be?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have an idea, but I want definite data. T do not want any guesswork about it.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is right here.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The government has it, and they have never given it to us. I ask that it be given, as a matter of right, to the membership of this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will permit me, I will tell him just what we expected would happen when we brought this in. We supposed that the opposition would ask me, as Minister of Finance, how the sum of approximately $1,450,000,000 was made up, and that I would tell him. I would give that in lump sums; such sums, for example, as six hundred and sixty-six millions, some hundreds of thousands, some odd dollars for the army; whereupon, I expected, in all probability some member of the opposition, probably the leader of the opposition, would say, "How is that made up?", and the Minister of National Defence would tell him in so far as he could, without divulging military secrets or giving information to the enemy. I thought that possibly the opposition would go through the whole sum in that way.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Well, we
are going to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We were prepared to give that information. I made it very clear at the outset that these were not ordinary estimates and that there would not be anything definite about them-as there is in ordinary estimates -nor were we bound to spend not more than the sums which we would mention. There is a certain amount of vagueness and looseness about the amounts which enter into a war appropriation bill. But we have not been withholding a single thing. We just wanted to know what the opposition required, and we would give it in so far as it was possible.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Our minds are coming together very rapidly. In other words, the minister was saying that it was not the duty of the government to give these figures at all; it was our duty to pry them out of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do suggest that, as trustees of the people of this country, as guardians of the public treasury, as tax-collectors of the people of this country, it is their duty to give an accounting without being asked to do it. Any trustee is bound to give an accounting to his cestui que trust.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: An accounting!

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I understand the implications of the minister's statement. I understand his implication is that the opposition has been derelict in its duty. I deny that absolutely.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I believe they have been.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: All right. I thought that was exactly the position the minister was taking. Well, better late than never.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Well, go ahead.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We want the detail of this, and we will ask to have it given to us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: How much?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The whole thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No, sir.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Except
those with respect to which I have already suggested that I would be quite agreeable to the reservation the minister made. If it is a secret fund

and yet I can scarcely imagine such a situation-how far is this matter of secrecy to go? I should like to think over the implications of that. What is the necessity for secrecy? In what respect? I assume it applies to $655,000,000. I deduce that from the statement of the Minister of Finance, and I do not know enough about it to know what would be secret and what 'would not. But we will find out before we are through.
How can we know if the thing is not given to us? I resent the suggestion that, in order that these details may be given, we must ask for them. That is not a principle of responsible government. That is a denial, a negation of the principle of responsible government. It is fascism in an incipient form.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is a waste of time, too.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Certainly it is a waste of time. I would not wish to hold up this resolution if I thought that to do so would delay the government's war effort. If delay would bring any aid or comfort to the enemy, if it would help Hitler to lick England or to invade Canada, I would say "Pass the resolution this minute." But nothing like that is going to happen, and no

War Appropriation Bill
argument can be based upon that supposition. I see now that it is based on the theory that there is to be non-disclosure of fact unless it is pried out of the government. That is the theory of the government's war appropriation resolution. Mr. Chairman, that is not good enough for the Canadian people. It is not only not good enough for the people's representatives who sit on this side; it is not good enough for hon. gentlemen who sit opposite or who sit in the corners of this chamber to my right and left. Let us have an end of this attempted suppression of the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, all this
language is quite unwarranted and quite unj ustified.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is a histrionic display which surprises me very much.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I hope the minister liked it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I certainly did not experience any feeling of uneasiness or discomfort as it
proceeded.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
As long
as the minister has a crowd behind him, he is as brave as a lion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I was not thinking about that aspect at all. The leader of the opposition said, why does the government not come forward and account? In the speech with which I opened this debate I stated exactly low much money had been spent to the end of January and how much money we anticipated would be spent by the end of the fiscal year; and, with regard to the coming year, I gave a total. It is only the total which we are asking the committee to vote; we are not asking the committee to vote any particular items.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
All the
more reason why we should have the items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Perhaps it was no more the opposition's duty than it was that of any other hon. members-although that is what they are there for. But if the opposition, instead of launching this curious campaign of editorial writing and attacks on my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply, had exercised a little bit of judgment and applied a few business principles to the examination of these amounts, they would have had this information long, long ago. When was there the time to give this information before this loud onslaught was delivered? When have we been asked for the information? We have been giving the information in large sums,
totals, and we have not been asked for anything else. When the hon. gentleman speaks about suppression of facts and the government waiting till the facts are pried out of them, he is dealing in old-line stuff which does not fool a single member of this committee a single minute.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You ought to know. Between 1930 and 1935 that is the sort of thing you fellows put over every day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There wasn't a war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, there was an economic war just as serious as this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The conditions were not like the conditions now.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Pretty bad.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If the opposition had told us a week or ten days ago what detail they wanted I would have tried to supply it, and if I could not I would have got my colleagues, the service ministers, to do it. But instead of that we have been listening to speeches. We have not been asked questions until this afternoon, and now we are not being asked questions but are being treated to a display of attempted parliamentary eloquence by the leader of the opposition, in which he says he is going to ask questions. What is the information the hon. gentleman wants?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Far from the facts bearing out the minister's suggestion as to what we should be doing, I would point out that I have had on the order paper since February 24 a question which his colleague the Minister of National Defence could answer:	.
1.	How many regiments are now included in the reserve army of Canada?
2.	What is the annual cost to Canada of pay and allowances of reserve army who are on full-time pay?
That had a distinct bearing on the matters under discussion now, and I have been keen to get an answer. In view of the fact that this question has been on the order paper since February 24, I cannot see how the Minister of Finance can say that we have not asked for information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I meant in the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should like to answer the question asked by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), which started all the discussion. I believe I stated as I sat down that I was prepared to answer questions now or later, and the first question with reference to the matter came from the member for Weyburn. It was a proper one. He asked whether I had information and whether I could give it now or would prefer to give it at some other time. I have consulted with
War Appropriation Bill

the Minister of Finance and he states that this is the proper time to deal with it. It could be dealt with again on the bill but now is the proper time to take it up.
So far as general information is concerned, I think it would be well to put the figures on Hansard this evening so that hon. members might have it before them between now and Monday.
The amount expended in my department is very small as compared with the total amount, but it will give some idea of the information in a part of the service in which I do not think there are any items that are secret. I believe that all the items in my department can be given to the members and to the public. I will read the general figures which will give an outline of the expenditures.
Taking departmental administration, the expenditures to January 31, 1941, amounted to $24,083.35.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister is giving the figures since the department was set up?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes. The amount
expended was the sum I have just mentioned and the estimated expenditure to the end of the financial year, March 31, 1941, is $16,24594. The total expenditure for 1940-41 is $40,329.29 and the estimated expenditure for the next year is $65,290.
For human resources, the first item is national registration, the amount expended to January 31, 1941, being $792,480.41. The estimated expenditure to the end of the year is $128,007.41. The total is $920,487.82. The estimated expenditure for the next year is SI,000. It is just a matter of keeping the records up to date.
Next is the bureau of statistics. As hon. members know, the bureau is in the Department of Trade and Commerce but it is doing work for us. It is not the intention of this department to set up any new branches where there is a branch already in existence which can do the particular work, and we use the bureau of statistics for all statistical work. This year the expenditure up to January 31, 1941, was $193,069.94 while the estimated expenditure to the end of the year is $153,454.49. The total is $346,524.43. For the next year the estimate is $129,360, which will again be only a matter of keeping up to date those records which I produced last evening.
The next item is recruiting. The expenditure to January 31, is $217,770.57. The estimated expenditure to the end of March 1941, is $498,472.90.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does that include transportation?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does it include transportation both ways, to and from the camp?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No. After they go to
the camps the national defence takes care of it. The total for recruiting for 1940-41 is $716,243.47, and the estimated expenditure for 1941-42 is $547,040.
With all due respect, I would venture to say that these figures are smaller than my hon. friend thought they would be, so far as our department is concerned. The next item is human and material resources. The expenditure to January 31, 1941, is $3,809.88. The estimated expenditure to March 31, 1941, is $34,445.82. The total is $38,255.70, and the estimated expenditure for 1941-42 is $63,210.
Next we come to voluntary services. The expenditure to January 31, 1941 is $8,434.99. The expenditure to the end of the year is $12,343.17. The total for 1940-41 is $20,778.16, and the estimated expenditure for 1941-42 is $27,080.
The last item is publicity. The expenditure to January 31-that is to say, the actual moneys paid out-amounted to $105,173.30. The estimated expenditure to the end of the year is $334,000.33. The total for 1940-41 is $439,173.63, and we estimate for next year a little more than double that amount, $956,420.
The total expenditure, 1940-41, is $2,521,792.50, and the estimated expenditure for 1941-42 is $1,789,400.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I wish to thank the minister for the break-down. I must say, however, that he is hardly fair in the statement he made. As I remember this procedure last year, when a similar resolution was brought down providing for $700,000,000, he first of all presented a general break-down of that figure and then each minister whose department was involved gave a statement of general policy and a break-down of the figure as it related to his department. If I remember correctly that was the policy followed last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I was not the minister then.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: By the present Minister of National Defence.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He certainly got under the skin of the government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
All right, I am glad. I am
supposed to foe one of those meek people who take it lying down. I say that there is no suggestion of suppression. It is not a fair statement to make such a suggestion. I understood my hon. friends wanted to get on with this resolution. They are entitled to all information possible as to past expenditure; as to the future we can tell them as best we can what the programme is, what we are trying to work out, but I think that is all. When you come to hang up the dollar sign in front of it, it is much more difficult than they think. Therefore I am here ready to give all the information I can in connection with any particular function, unless it is something secret, and there is not much that is, but it is subject to so many factors and events that it is not much use. There are so many unknown factors which one cannot take into account beforehand, and which must be considered as constituting conditions and reservations that it is difficult to give accurate information.
The hon. member for Souris said he had not received any answer to his question. I say to my hon. friend that I personally called him no less than three times on the telephone at his room with reference to that very question. I should have written him a letter or rose in my place in the house; I am sorry. But the form of my hon. friend's question makes it difficult to know just what information he wants.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am sorry. But I was in the house each time the minister asked that the question stand.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
He asks:
What is the annual cost to Canada of pay and allowances of reserve army who are on full-time pay?
War Appropriation Bill

I think my hon. friend is asking for the pay and allowances of those of the reserve army who are working in connection with the reserve units. The question of pay and allowances of those in the reserve army involves much more than that, because many are on a camp staff somewhere else altogether. They may be in England. I wanted to ask my hon. friend just what he wanted, and that is why he has not been given the information before.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I wanted the estimated cost of the reserve army in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That is not what the
question says at all. The only people who are on full-time pay are the officers who are working with the units, it might be a quartermaster sergeant or some sergeant at headquarters. There are those of the reserve office who are on full-time pay and allowances who are not working with and whose duties do not concern the reserve army at all; they are working in connection with some staff duties. I have the information in two ways; I thought my hon. friend was really concerned with the reserve units, but I did not want to give an answer and have him say I gave the wrong information.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: With regard to what the minister has just said, is it necessary that those officers or non-commissioned officers so employed be of a category which would take them into the active service army?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It depends upon what
the job is.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Will the Minister of Finance give us for the other war departments a statement and break-down similar to the one that has been placed on the record by the Minister of National War Services? These figures are large; they are numerous; I have a pretty good head for figures, but I cannot remember them; I certainly would like to investigate and examine them. I think that by consent we could eliminate discussion about a good many of these items, if this were done. Certainly I do not want to go through the whole array.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I will give, and put it on Hansard so that hon. gentlemen can have it for Monday', a list of the amounts which make up the total-I said approximately 81,450.000,000; it is almost exactly $1,400,000,000. I will put them on Hansard now.

speechtext:
Or we
could take it as read, and save time. If the minister has a spare copy and could send it to my office, I should be greatly obliged.

speechtext: I can get a copy for my hon. friend but I do not have it here. This will not give the kind of break-down that the Minister of National War Services just gave the committee; this will give much larger items.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

considerations I wanted the house to have at the time the figures were given. One, of course, was with reference to the uncertainty about deliveries. That always would have to be taken into account. I think the other uncertainty was as to the nature of the developments in the war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think that is very reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Those are the qualifications; and with those three considerations these are the figures. It was because of the qualifications that I did not want to ask the house for $1,460,000,000. I thought that to ask for $1,300,000,000 was a reasonable thing to do under the circumstances.

The Late John Hall Kelly

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence if he will break down the figures for the army into the amount spent last year for the non-permanent active militia; the amount spent on the active service force; the amount spent on the trainees; the amount spent on the administration of general headquarters; the amount spent on the administration of the different districts; the amount spent on ordnance and stores; the amount spent for construction and repairs, and the amount spent for transportation. I should also like a break-down of what it is expected will be spent during the coming year under the same divisions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am not sure that I have the expenditures for the coming year in that form. The way I have them here is in formations or functions, but I shall endeavour to see if the information can be put in the other form. My hon. friend has given us quite an order there.
Progress reported.
Mr. CRERAR moved the adjournment of the house.
What will be the business on Monday?

The business on Monday will be a continuation of the discussion on this resolution. If we get it out of committee, and the house is agreeable, we would like to proceed with the bill. Should that not be possible, we will take up the resolutions on the order paper in the name of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the Minister of Mines and Resources and the Minister of Public Works, also the second readings on the order paper. None of them is very contentious, and probably they will pass quickly. I do not wish to imply that this necessarily will be the order in which these matters will be taken up.
But generally speaking?
Generally speaking.
Is this all the auditor general's report we are going to have to help us look into these matters? If so, it will take a long time to get through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is only the one report for the year.

I am asking if this is
the only report we are going to get from the auditor general with reference to expenditures for the year ending March 31, 1940.

There really is not anything at all in this report. If we are compelled to ask all the questions we may find necessary, I can see us sitting here until next Christmas.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I am pleased to hear there is nothing in the report.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at
six p.m.
Monday, March 10, 1941.
